arXiv:astro-ph/0608371v1 [astro-ph] 17 Aug 2006

Electron thermal conductivity owing to collisions between degenerate electrons

P. S. Shternin and D. G. Yakovlev Affiliation: Ioffe Physical Technical Institute, Politekhnicheskaya 26, 194021 Saint-Petersburg, Russia
August 24, 2026
Abstract

We calculate the thermal conductivity of electrons produced by electron-electron Coulomb scattering in a strongly degenerate electron gas taking into account the Landau damping of transverse plasmons. The Landau damping strongly reduces this conductivity in the domain of ultrarelativistic electrons at temperatures below the electron plasma temperature. In the inner crust of a neutron star at temperatures T≲107T\lesssim 10^{7} K this thermal conductivity completely dominates over the electron conductivity due to electron-ion (electron-phonon) scattering and becomes competitive with the the electron conductivity due to scattering of electrons by impurity ions.

I Introduction

The electron thermal conductivity is an important kinetic property of plasmas in experimental devices, in metals and semiconductors and in astrophysical objects. It has been studied for a long time and described in textbooks (see, e.g., Ziman [1], Lifshitz and Pitaevskiĭ [2]). We will show that some aspects of this problem have to be revised.

Specifically, we will consider the thermal conductivity of degenerate electrons. It is important in metals, semiconductors as well as in degenerate cores of evolved stars (giants, supergiants and, most importantly, white dwarfs), and in envelopes of neutron stars. It is needed to study cooling of white dwarfs (e.g., Prada Moroni and Straniero [3]) and nuclear explosions of massive white dwarfs as type Ia supernovae (e.g., Baraffe, Heger and Woosley [4]). In neutron star envelopes it is required for many reasons — for simulating cooling of isolated neutron stars (see, e.g., Lattimer et al. [5], Gnedin, Yakovlev and Potekhin [6], Page, Geppert and Weber [7]); for studying heat propagation and thermal relaxation in a neutron star envelope in response to the various processes of crustal energy release. In particular, these processes include pulsar glitches (e.g., Larson and Link [8], and references therein), deep crustal heating of accreting neutron stars in soft X-ray transients (e.g., Ushomirsky and Rutledge [9]), superbursts as powerful nuclear explosions at the base of the outer crust of an accreting neutron star (e.g., Strohmayer and Bildsten [10]; Page and Cumming [11]).

It is well known, that the electrons give the main contribution into the thermal conductivity of strongly degenerate matter. Their thermal conductivity can be written as

κe=π2​T​kB2​ne3​me∗​νe,νe=νe​i+νe​e.\kappa_{e}={\pi^{2}Tk_{\rm B}^{2}n_{e}\over 3m_{e}^{*}\nu_{e}},\quad\nu_{e}=\nu_{ei}+\nu_{ee}. (1)

Here, TT is the temperature, kBk_{\rm B} is the Boltzmann constant, nen_{e} is the number density of electrons, me∗=μ/c2m_{e}^{*}=\mu/c^{2}, μ\mu is the electron chemical potential (including the rest-mass term), and νe\nu_{e} is the total effective electron collision frequency. The latter frequency is the sum of the partial collision frequencies νe​i\nu_{ei} and νe​e\nu_{ee}. In νe​i\nu_{ei} we include all collisions of electrons mediated by their interactions with ions (direct Coulomb scattering of electrons by ions in an ion gas or liquid; electron-phonon scattering in an ion crystal and electron scattering by impurity ions at low temperatures). Evidently, Eq. (1) can be rewritten as

1κe=1κe​i+1κe​e,κe​i=π2​T​kB2​ne3​me∗​νe​i,\displaystyle{1\over\kappa_{e}}={1\over\kappa_{ei}}+{1\over\kappa_{ee}},\quad\kappa_{ei}={\pi^{2}Tk_{\rm B}^{2}n_{e}\over 3m_{e}^{*}\nu_{ei}},
κe​e=π2​T​kB2​ne3​me∗​νe​e,\displaystyle\kappa_{ee}={\pi^{2}Tk_{\rm B}^{2}n_{e}\over 3m_{e}^{*}\nu_{ee}}, (2)

where the partial conductivities κe​i\kappa_{ei} and κe​e\kappa_{ee} are determined, respectively, by the e​iei and e​eee collisions.

It is widely believed that the dominant contribution into κe\kappa_{e} comes from the e​iei collisions. The associated partial conductivity κe​i\kappa_{ei} has been studied in a number of papers (e.g., Potekhin et al. [12], Gnedin et al. [6] and references therein). The partial thermal conductivity κe​e\kappa_{ee} owing to the e​eee collisions was calculated by Lampe [13], Flowers and Itoh [14], Urpin and Yakovlev [15], and Timmes [16]. These calculations were summarized by Potekhin et al. [12]. The main result was that the e​eee collisions are mainly negligible, except for a hot low-density plasma of light elements (from hydrogen to carbon) with the temperature a few times lower than the electron degeneracy temperature (in that case the e​eee collisions did affect κe\kappa_{e} but never dominated as long as the electrons were degenerate; see Lampe [13]; Urpin and Yakovlev [15]).

However, all these calculations have neglected an important effect of the Landau damping of the e​eee interaction owing to the exchange of transverse plasmons. In the context of transport properties of dense matter this effect was studied by Heiselberg and Pethick [17] for degenerate quark plasmas. Similar effects have recently been analyzed by Jaikumar, Gale and Page [18] for neutrino bremsstrahlung radiation in the e​eee collisions. Here we reconsider κe​e\kappa_{ee} including the effects of the Landau damping and show that κe​e\kappa_{ee} is actually much more important than thought before.

II Formalism

We analyze the thermal conductivity κe​e\kappa_{ee} of strongly degenerate electrons under the conditions that the electrons constitute an almost ideal and uniform Fermi gas and collide between themselves and with plasma ions. Although the results will be more important for ultrarelativistic electrons, our consideration will be general and valid for both, relativistic and non-relativistic, cases. We will use the same standard variational approach with the simplest trial non-equilibrium electron distribution function as Flowers and Itoh [14]. The calculations are similar to those performed by Heiselberg and Pethick [17] for the thermal conductivity of quarks; thus we omit the details.

Following Heiselberg and Pethick [17] we have

νe​e\displaystyle\nu_{ee} =\displaystyle= 3​ℏ38​ve​pe2​(kB​T)3​∫d​𝒑1​d​𝒑2​d​𝒑1′​d​𝒑2′(2​π​ℏ)12\displaystyle{3\hbar^{3}\over 8v_{e}p_{e}^{2}(k_{\rm B}T)^{3}}\,\int{{\rm d}\bm{p}_{1}\,{\rm d}\bm{p}_{2}\,{\rm d}\bm{p}^{\prime}_{1}\,{\rm d}\bm{p}^{\prime}_{2}\over(2\pi\hbar)^{12}} (3)

W⁡(12|1′​2′)\displaystyle W(12|1^{\prime}2^{\prime}) =\displaystyle= 4​(2​π​ℏ)6​δ​(ε1′+ε2′−ε1−ε2)\displaystyle 4\,(2\pi\hbar)^{6}\,\delta(\varepsilon^{\prime}_{1}+\varepsilon^{\prime}_{2}-\varepsilon_{1}-\varepsilon_{2})\, (4)
×δ⁡(𝒑1′+𝒑2′−𝒑1−𝒑2)​|Mf​i|2,\displaystyle\times\delta(\bm{p}^{\prime}_{1}+\bm{p}^{\prime}_{2}-\bm{p}_{1}-\bm{p}_{2})\,|M_{fi}|^{2},

|Mf​i|2|M_{fi}|^{2} being the squared matrix element summed over electron spin states. The symmetry factors required to avoid double counting of the same initial and final electron states are also included into |Mf​i|2|M_{fi}|^{2}.

The multi-dimensional integral (3) is simplified further using the standard angular-energy decomposition (separating integrations over particle energies and orientations of their momenta; e.g., Shapiro and Teukolsky [19]). Because the electrons are strongly degenerate, they can participate in thermal conduction only if their energies are close to the Fermi level. Accordingly, their momenta can be placed at the Fermi surface in angular integrals whenever possible. Characteristic energy transfers ℏ​ω≡ε1′−ε1\hbar\omega\equiv\varepsilon^{\prime}_{1}-\varepsilon_{1} in collisions of strongly degenerate particles are small, ℏ​ω≲kB​T\hbar\omega\lesssim k_{\rm B}T. Momentum transfers ℏ​𝒒≡𝒑1′−𝒑1\hbar\bm{q}\equiv\bm{p}^{\prime}_{1}-\bm{p}_{1} are also small, ℏ​q≪pe\hbar q\ll p_{e}, owing to a long-range nature of the Coulomb interaction. We will use this small-momentum-transfer approximation throughout the paper. Typical values of ℏ​q\hbar q are determined by plasma screening of the Coulomb interaction.

The plasma screening was thoroughly analyzed by Heiselberg and Pethick [17]. These authors studied quark-quark interaction through one-gluon exchange in the weak-coupling limit which is very similar to the Coulomb interaction in an ordinary plasma. The matrix element for an e​eee scattering event is Mf​i=Mf​i(1)+Mf​i(2)M_{fi}=M^{(1)}_{fi}+M^{(2)}_{fi}, where Mf​i(1)M^{(1)}_{fi} and Mf​i(2)M^{(2)}_{fi} correspond to the channels 1→1′;2→2′1\to 1^{\prime};2\to 2^{\prime} and 1→2′;2→1′1\to 2^{\prime};2\to 1^{\prime}, respectively. For instance,

Mf​i(1)∝J1′​1(0)​J2′​2(0)q2+Πl−𝑱t​1′​1⋅𝑱t​2′​2q2−ω2/c2+Πt,M^{(1)}_{fi}\propto\frac{J_{1^{\prime}1}^{(0)}J_{2^{\prime}2}^{(0)}}{q^{2}+\Pi_{l}}-\frac{\bm{J}_{t1^{\prime}1}\bm{\cdot}\bm{J}_{t2^{\prime}2}}{q^{2}-\omega^{2}/c^{2}+\Pi_{t}}, (5)

where Je′​e(ν)=(Je′​e(0),𝑱e′​e)=c⁡(u¯e′​γν​ue)J_{e^{\prime}e}^{(\nu)}=(J_{e^{\prime}e}^{(0)},\bm{J}_{e^{\prime}e})=c\,(\bar{u}_{e^{\prime}}\gamma^{\nu}u_{e}) is the transition 4-current (ν\nu=0, 1, 2, 3), 𝑱t​e′​e\bm{J}_{te^{\prime}e} is the component of 𝑱e′​e\bm{J}_{e^{\prime}e} transverse to 𝒒\bm{q}, γν\gamma^{\nu} is a Dirac matrix, ueu_{e} is a normalized electron bispinor (u¯e​ue=2​me​c2\bar{u}_{e}u_{e}=2m_{e}c^{2}), and u¯e\bar{u}_{e} is a Dirac conjugate (see, e.g., Berestetskiĭ, Lifshitz and Pitaevskii [20]). The longitudinal component of 𝑱e′​e\bm{J}_{e^{\prime}e} (parallel to 𝒒\bm{q}) is related to the time-like (charge density) component Je′​e(0)J_{e^{\prime}e}^{(0)} via current continuity equation; it is excluded from Eq. (5), see Ref. [17].

The polarization functions Πl\Pi_{l} and Πt\Pi_{t} in Eq. (5) depend on ω\omega and qq and describe the plasma screening of the e​eee interaction through the exchange of longitudinal and transverse plasmons, respectively. In the classical limit (ℏ​q≪pe\hbar q\ll p_{e} and ℏ​ω≪ve​pe\hbar\omega\ll v_{e}p_{e}), taking into account the polarization produced by degenerate electrons in the first-order random phase approximation, one has (e.g., Alexandrov, Bogdankevich and Rukhadze [21])

Πl=q02​χl​(x),Πt=(q0​ve/c)2​χt​(x),\Pi_{l}=q_{0}^{2}\,\chi_{l}(x),\qquad\Pi_{t}=(q_{0}v_{e}/c)^{2}\,\chi_{t}(x), (6)

where x=ω/(q​ve)x=\omega/(qv_{e}),

χl​(x)\displaystyle\chi_{l}(x) =\displaystyle= 1−x2​ln⁡(x+1x−1),\displaystyle 1-{x\over 2}\,\ln\left(x+1\over x-1\right),
χt​(x)\displaystyle\chi_{t}(x) =\displaystyle= x22+x⁡(1−x2)4​ln⁡(x+1x−1),\displaystyle{x^{2}\over 2}+{x(1-x^{2})\over 4}\,\ln\left(x+1\over x-1\right), (7)

with

ℏ2​q02=4​e2​pe2/(π​ℏ​ve),\hbar^{2}q_{0}^{2}={4e^{2}p_{e}^{2}/(\pi\hbar v_{e})}, (8)

q0q_{0} being the ordinary Thomas-Fermi electron screening wavenumber. Particularly, in the limit of ω→0\omega\to 0 and ω/q≪ve\omega/q\ll v_{e} we have

χl=1,χt=i​π​ω/(4​q​ve).\chi_{l}=1,\qquad\chi_{t}=i\,\pi\omega/(4qv_{e}). (9)

According to Eqs. (5) and (6), the plasma screening of the e​eee current interaction via the exchange of transverse plasmons (the second term in Eq. (5)) is different from the screening of the charge interaction via the exchange of longitudinal plasmons (the first term). The difference results from the difference of the polarization functions Πt\Pi_{t} and Πl\Pi_{l} and has been neglected in all previous calculations of the electron thermal conductivity (where one has commonly set Πt=Πl=q02\Pi_{t}=\Pi_{l}=q_{0}^{2}, and q2−(ω/c)2+Πt=q2+q02q^{2}-(\omega/c)^{2}+\Pi_{t}=q^{2}+q_{0}^{2}). Naturally, this difference is expected to be small for non-relativistic electrons (ve≪cv_{e}\ll c), where the transverse current interaction term is small in the matrix element. We will see that the difference becomes important for relativistic electrons (ve≈cv_{e}\approx c).

Let us recall that the functions Πl\Pi_{l} and Πt\Pi_{t} have real parts which describe plasmon refraction, and imaginary parts which describe plasmon absorption. In the e​eee scattering we deal with low-energy virtual plasmons, ℏ​ω≲kB​T\hbar\omega\lesssim k_{\rm B}T. As seen from Eq. (9), longitudinal plasmons undergo refraction which results in the Debye-type (Thomas-Fermi) screening of the Coulomb interaction, with the screening momentum (inverse screening length) q0q_{0}. As for transverse plasmons, they mainly undergo collisionless absorption (that is the Landau damping) by degenerate electrons. Their effect is drastically different from the effect of longitudinal plasmons.

The calculations similar to those in Ref. [17] lead to the following expressions for the e​eee collision frequency and thermal conductivity,

νe​e=36​ne​α2​ℏ2​c​I​(u,θ)π​me∗​kB​T,κe​e=π3​kB3​T2108​α2​ℏ2​c​I​(u,θ).\nu_{ee}={36n_{e}\alpha^{2}\hbar^{2}cI(u,\theta)\over\pi m_{e}^{*}k_{\rm B}T},\qquad\kappa_{ee}={\pi^{3}k_{\rm B}^{3}T^{2}\over 108\alpha^{2}\hbar^{2}cI(u,\theta)}. (10)

Here, α=e2/ℏ​c\alpha=e^{2}/\hbar c is the fine structure constant, and

is a dimensionless function of two variables,

u≡ve/c,θ=ℏ​ve​q0/(kB​T)=3​Tp​e/T,u\equiv v_{e}/c,\qquad\theta=\hbar v_{e}q_{0}/(k_{\rm B}T)=\sqrt{3}T_{pe}/T, (12)

Both components of the matrix element, Mf​i(1)M^{(1)}_{fi} and Mf​i(2)M^{(2)}_{fi}, give equal contributions into Eq. (11), and the interference term is negligibly small because of the small-momentum-transfer approximation. Furthermore, w=ℏ​ω/kB​Tw=\hbar\omega/k_{\rm B}T; ϕ\phi is the angle between 𝒑1​t\bm{p}_{1t} and 𝒑2​t\bm{p}_{2t}, the components of 𝒑1\bm{p}_{1} and 𝒑2\bm{p}_{2} transverse to 𝒒\bm{q}; and the integration over ϕ\phi is trivial. Equations (10) and (11) are natural generalizations of Eqs. (58) and (59) of Heiselberg and Pethick [17] to the case of a degenerate gas of particles of arbitrary degree of relativity (in our case v/cv/c may be arbitrary while in Ref. [17] v=cv=c). The difference of numerical factors in the expressions for κ\kappa in our Eq. (10) and in Eq. (58) of Ref. [17] (108 versus 24) stems from the difference of physical systems under consideration (an electron gas versus a gas of light quarks interacting through gluon exchange).

III Four regimes of electron-electron collisions

Thus the collision frequency and the thermal conductivity (10) are solely determined by the electron number density and the temperature. Their calculation reduces to the calculation of the function I⁡(u,θ)I(u,\theta) from Eq. (11). Clearly, the function can be written as

I=Il+It+Il​t,I=I_{l}+I_{t}+I_{lt}, (13)

where IlI_{l} is the contribution from the e​eee interaction via the exchange of longitudinal plasmons (the first term in the squared modulus); ItI_{t} comes from the interaction via the exchange of transverse plasmons (the second term); and Il​tI_{lt} is the mixed term.

The analysis reveals four regimes (I–IV) of e​eee collisions in a strongly degenerate electron gas. These regimes are summarized in Table 1. The regimes I and II are realized for non-relativistic electrons, while in the regimes III and IV electrons are ultrarelativistic. The regimes I and III take place for sufficiently high temperatures T≳Tp​eT\gtrsim T_{pe}, at which the Pauli principle does not restrict energy transfers between colliding electrons (ℏ​ω<kB​T\hbar\omega<k_{\rm B}T; see, e.g., Lampe [13], especially his Fig. 1). The regimes II and IV refer to a colder electron gas, where energy transfers are essentially limited by the Pauli blocking (e.g., Lampe [13] and Flowers and Itoh [14]).

The analysis of Eq. (11) gives the following asymptotic values of II in the different regimes.

In the regime I (where u≲1u\lesssim 1 and θ≲1\theta\lesssim 1)

Il\displaystyle I_{l} =\displaystyle= 1u​(215​ln⁡1θ+0.1657),\displaystyle{1\over u}\,\left({2\over 15}\ln{1\over\theta}+0.1657\right),
It\displaystyle I_{t} =\displaystyle= u3​(8315​ln⁡1θ​u+0.05067),\displaystyle u^{3}\,\left({8\over 315}\ln{1\over\theta u}+0.05067\right),
Il​t\displaystyle I_{lt} =\displaystyle= u⁡(8105​ln⁡1θ+0.1236).\displaystyle u\,\left({8\over 105}\ln{1\over\theta}+0.1236\right). (14)

The logarithmic terms in brackets represent Coulomb logarithms, while the second terms are the corrections calculated using the standard technique [13]. The leading contribution comes from IlI_{l}. It was calculated by Lampe [13], with a slightly less accurate correction term (1.30×2/15≈0.1731.30\times 2/15\approx 0.173 from his Eqs. (5.22) and (5.23), instead of our 0.1657). Retaining this term in the regime I, one has I=IlI=I_{l} and

κe​e=5​π3​kB3​T2​ve72​α2​ℏ2​c2​[ln⁡(1/θ)+1.242].\kappa_{ee}={5\pi^{3}k_{\rm B}^{3}T^{2}v_{e}\over 72\alpha^{2}\hbar^{2}c^{2}\,[\ln(1/\theta)+1.242]}. (15)

Note that for ItI_{t} the regime I extends to lower temperatures T∼u​Tp​eT\sim uT_{pe}, than for IlI_{l} and Il​tI_{lt}, but this circumstance does not affect noticeably the thermal conductivity κe​e\kappa_{ee} because ItI_{t} is relatively insignificant in the given regime.

In the regime III (where u≈1u\approx 1 and θ≲1\theta\lesssim 1),

Il\displaystyle I_{l}\penalty\ =\displaystyle= 2​It=215​ln⁡1θ+0.1657,\displaystyle 2I_{t}={2\over 15}\,\ln{1\over\theta}+0.1657,
Il​t\displaystyle I_{lt} =\displaystyle= 215​ln⁡1θ+0.1399,\displaystyle{2\over 15}\,\ln{1\over\theta}+0.1399,
I\displaystyle I\penalty\ =\displaystyle= 13​ln⁡1θ+0.3884.\displaystyle{1\over 3}\,\ln{1\over\theta}+0.3884. (16)

Again, the logarithmic terms are Coulomb logarithms and the second terms are corrections. In this case, all terms (IlI_{l}, ItI_{t}, and Il​tI_{lt}) give comparable contributions into II. The asymptote of II in this regime was obtained by Heiselberg and Pethick [17] (their Eq. (60), with a slightly less accurate correction factor 0.30 instead of our 0.3884) in their studies of quark plasma. For an electron plasma, the conductivity κe​e\kappa_{ee} in the regime III was calculated by Urpin and Yakovlev [15]. Their result is equivalent to Eq. (16) for II but with less accurate correction (ln⁡(2)/3≈0.231\ln(2)/3\approx 0.231 instead of 0.3884) because they erroneously used the approximation of static longitudinal electron screening of the Coulomb interaction in all terms (with Πl=Πt=q02\Pi_{l}=\Pi_{t}=q_{0}^{2} in Eq. (6)). Employing II from Eq. (16) in the regime III we obtain

κe​e=π3​kB3​T236​α2​ℏ2​c​[ln⁡(1/θ)+1.165].\kappa_{ee}={\pi^{3}k_{\rm B}^{3}T^{2}\over 36\alpha^{2}\hbar^{2}c\,[\ln(1/\theta)+1.165]}. (17)

In the regimes II and IV (where θ≳1\theta\gtrsim 1 and u≤1u\leq 1 is arbitrary) we have

Il=π515​u​θ3,It=2​ζ​(3)​uθ2,Il​t=ξθ8/3​u1/3,\displaystyle I_{l}={\pi^{5}\over 15u\theta^{3}},\quad I_{t}=2\zeta(3)\,{u\over\theta^{2}},\quad I_{lt}={\xi\over\theta^{8/3}}\,u^{1/3}, (18)
ξ=(2​π)2/33​Γ​(143)​ζ​(113)≈18.52,\displaystyle\xi={(2\pi)^{2/3}\over 3}\,\Gamma\left(14\over 3\right)\,\zeta\left(11\over 3\right)\approx 18.52,

where ζ⁡(z)\zeta(z) is the Riemann zeta function (with ζ⁡(3)=1.202\zeta(3)=1.202) and Γ⁡(z)\Gamma(z) is the gamma function. The expression for ItI_{t} (with u=1u=1) was obtained by Heiselberg and Pethick [17] for an ultrarelativistic quark plasma.

The asymptotic expressions (18) are derived from Eq. (11) with the screening functions χl\chi_{l} and χt\chi_{t} given by Eq. (9). In this approximation the screening of the e​eee interaction via the exchange of longitudinal plasmons (the first part of the matrix element in Eq. (5)) is described by q2+Πl≈q2+q02q^{2}+\Pi_{l}\approx q^{2}+q_{0}^{2}, which is equivalent to the static Debye-type screening with the screening wavenumber qscr,l=q0q_{{\rm scr},l}=q_{0}. The screening via the exchange of transverse plasmons (the second part of the matrix element) is more complicated. It is described by the denominator term q2−ω2/c2+Πt≈q2+i​q02​π​ω​ve/(4​q​c2)q^{2}-\omega^{2}/c^{2}+\Pi_{t}\approx q^{2}+iq_{0}^{2}\pi\omega v_{e}/(4qc^{2}) that represents the dynamical screening via the Landau damping of transverse plasmons, with ℏ​ω∼kB​T≪ve​ℏ​q\hbar\omega\sim k_{\rm B}T\ll v_{e}\hbar q (i.e., with low phase velocities ω/q≪ve\omega/q\ll v_{e}). In this case the effective screening wavenumber qscr,tq_{{\rm scr},t} is evidently given by qscr,t3∼q02​ω​ve/c2∼q02​kB​T​ve/(ℏ​c2)q^{3}_{{\rm scr},t}\sim q_{0}^{2}\omega v_{e}/c^{2}\sim q_{0}^{2}k_{\rm B}Tv_{e}/(\hbar c^{2}).

Using Eqs. (10) and (13) we can decompose the collision frequency νe​e\nu_{ee} into the same parts as II, νe​e=νe​e(l)+νe​e(t)+νe​e(l​t)\nu_{ee}=\nu_{ee}^{(l)}+\nu_{ee}^{(t)}+\nu_{ee}^{(lt)}. One can easily see, that in the regimes II and IV the partial frequency νe​e(l)\nu_{ee}^{(l)} can be estimated as νe​e(l)∼ne​α2​(kB​T)2/(ℏ​qscr,l3​μ)\nu_{ee}^{(l)}\sim n_{e}\alpha^{2}(k_{\rm B}T)^{2}/(\hbar q_{{\rm scr},l}^{3}\mu). The collision frequency νe​e(t)\nu_{ee}^{(t)} can be estimated as νe​e(t)∼u4​νe​e(l)\nu_{ee}^{(t)}\sim u^{4}\,\nu_{ee}^{(l)} by replacing qscr,l→qscr,tq_{{\rm scr},l}\to q_{{\rm scr},t}. The factor u4u^{4} takes into account the reduction of the e​eee interaction via transverse plasmons in the nonrelativistic electron gas. The quantity νe​e(l​t)\nu_{ee}^{(lt)} can be estimated as νe​e(l​t)∼u2​νe​e(l)\nu_{ee}^{(lt)}\sim u^{2}\,\nu_{ee}^{(l)} with qscr,l3→qscr,l2​qscr,tq_{{\rm scr},l}^{3}\to q_{{\rm scr},l}^{2}\,q_{{\rm scr},t}.

In the regime II, where θ≳1\theta\gtrsim 1 and u≪1u\ll 1, the exchange of longitudinal plasmons dominates, and we have I≈IlI\approx I_{l},

κe​e=5​ℏ​q03​ve436​π2​T​α2​c2.\kappa_{ee}={5\hbar q_{0}^{3}v_{e}^{4}\over 36\pi^{2}T\alpha^{2}c^{2}}. (19)

This leading part of κe​e\kappa_{ee} in the regime II was calculated by Lampe [13]. Note that the asymptotic expression (18) for ItI_{t} at u≪1u\ll 1 is actually valid not at T≲Tp​eT\lesssim T_{pe}, as the expressions for IlI_{l} and Il​tI_{lt}, but at lower T≲u​Tp​eT\lesssim uT_{pe}. However, this circumstance is relatively unimportant because it is IlI_{l} which dominates in the regime II.

In the regime IV, where θ≳1\theta\gtrsim 1 and u≈1u\approx 1, the exchange of transverse plasmons dominates, with I≈ItI\approx I_{t}, and

κe​e=π3​kB​c​q02216​ζ​(3)​α2.\kappa_{ee}={\pi^{3}k_{\rm B}cq_{0}^{2}\over 216\,\zeta(3)\alpha^{2}}. (20)

It is remarkable that in this regime κe​e\kappa_{ee} becomes temperature independent. This regime has been discussed in detail by Heiselberg and Pethick [17] for quark plasma. For the electron plasma, it was considered by Flowers and Itoh [14] and also by Urpin and Yakovlev [15] but both groups erroneously used the approximation of static longitudinal screening in all channels (χl=χt=1\chi_{l}=\chi_{t}=1) which strongly underestimates the efficiency of the plasma screening of the e​eee interaction in the ultrarelativistic electron gas. If that approximation were true, one would obtain νe​e(l)=νe​e(l​t)=2​νe​e(t)\nu_{ee}^{(l)}=\nu_{ee}^{(lt)}=2\nu_{ee}^{(t)} and νe​e=2.5​νe​e(l)\nu_{ee}=2.5\nu_{ee}^{(l)}, whereas in fact νe​e(l)≪νe​e(l​t)≪νe​e(t)\nu_{ee}^{(l)}\ll\nu_{ee}^{(lt)}\ll\nu_{ee}^{(t)} in the regime IV, and κe​e\kappa_{ee} is significantly lower than predicted by the previous calculations [14, 15].

Let us note that the temperature behavior of κe​e\kappa_{ee} (Table 1) corresponds to an ordinary Fermi-liquid (where κ∝1/T\kappa\propto 1/T; e.g., Baym and Pethick [22]) only in the regime II. In the regimes I and III the plasma is too warm (although degenerate) to reach the Fermi-liquid limit, where energy transfers between colliding particles are strongly restricted by the Pauli principle. In the regime IV the plasma is cold but the matrix element of the e​eee interaction essentially depends on energy transfers ℏ​ω\hbar\omega owing to the Landau damping of transverse plasmons which violates the Fermi-liquid behavior [17].

To facilitate applications, we have calculated the functions IlI_{l}, ItI_{t} and Il​tI_{lt} from Eq. (11) for a dense grid of uu and θ\theta and fitted the numerical data by analytic functions. We obtain

Il\displaystyle I_{l} =\displaystyle= 1u​(0.1587−0.025381+0.0435​θ)\displaystyle{1\over u}\,\left(0.1587-{0.02538\over 1+0.0435\,\theta}\right) (21)
×ln⁡(1+128.5637.1​θ+10.83​θ2+θ3).\displaystyle\times\ln\left(1+{128.56\over 37.1\,\theta+10.83\,\theta^{2}+\theta^{3}}\right).

Therefore, IlI_{l} is inversely proportional to uu, with the proportionality coefficient dependent solely on θ\theta. Furthermore,

It\displaystyle I_{t} =\displaystyle= u3​(2.404C+C2−2.404/C1+0.1​θ​u)\displaystyle u^{3}\,\left({2.404\over C}+{C_{2}-2.404/C\over 1+0.1\,\theta\,u}\right) (22)
×ln⁡(1+CA​θ​u+θ2​u2),\displaystyle\times\ln\left(1+{C\over A\,\theta\,u+\theta^{2}\,u^{2}}\right),

where A=20+450​u3A=20+450\,u^{3}, C=A​exp⁡(C1/C2)C=A\,\exp(C_{1}/C_{2}), C1=0.05067+0.03216​u2C_{1}=0.05067+0.03216\,u^{2}, and C2=0.0254+0.04127​u4C_{2}=0.0254+0.04127\,u^{4}. Finally,

Il​t\displaystyle I_{lt} =\displaystyle= u⁡(18.52​u2C+C2−18.52​u2/C1+0.1558​θB)\displaystyle u\,\left({18.52\,u^{2}\over C}+{C_{2}-18.52\,u^{2}/C\over 1+0.1558\,\theta^{B}}\right) (23)

These fit expressions reproduce also all asymptotic limits mentioned above. The maximum fit errors of IlI_{l}, ItI_{t}, and Il​tI_{lt} are, respectively, 0.2% (at u=0.61u=0.61 and θ=3.8\theta=3.8), 6.3% (at u=0.878u=0.878 and θ∼0.175\theta\sim 0.175, where the electrons become nondegenerate) and 8.4% (at u=0.19u=0.19 and θ=19\theta=19). The maximum fit error of the total function II in Eq. (13) is 2.5% (at u=0.924u=0.924 and θ=0.232\theta=0.232).

IV Discussion

Let us discuss the efficiency of e​eee collisions for thermal conduction in a degenerate electron gas. Figure 1 shows the temperature-density diagram for a dense matter. For certainty, we have adopted the model of cold-catalyzed (ground-state) matter. It is composed of electrons and ions (atomic nuclei) at densities smaller than the neutron drip density ρnd≈4×1011\rho_{\rm nd}\approx 4\times 10^{11} g cm-3 (the right vertical dotted line), with an addition of free neutrons at higher densities ρ\rho. The composition of the cold-catalyzed matter is taken from Haensel and Pichon [23] at ρ<ρnd\rho<\rho_{\rm nd} and from Negele and Vautherin [24] at higher ρ\rho. Weak first-oder phase transitions which accompany changes of ground-state nuclides with the growth of ρ\rho are smoothed out as described by Kaminker et al. [25]. At ρ≲108\rho\lesssim 10^{8} g cm-3 the ground-state matter is composed of iron (56Fe). The densities ρ≲109\rho\lesssim 10^{9} g cm-3 are appropriate for degenerate stellar cores of white dwarfs and evolved stars; the densities ρ≲1014\rho\lesssim 10^{14} are appropriate for envelopes (crusts) of neutron stars.

In Figure 1 we plot the electron degeneracy temperature TF=(μ−me​c2)/kBT_{\rm F}=(\mu-m_{e}c^{2})/k_{\rm B}, the electron plasma temperature Tp​eT_{pe}, the melting temperature of the ion crystal Tm≈Zi2​e2/(175​a​kB)T_{\rm m}\approx Z_{i}^{2}e^{2}/(175ak_{\rm B}), and the ion plasma temperature Tp​i=ℏ​ωp​i/kBT_{pi}=\hbar\omega_{pi}/k_{\rm B} (where ωp​i=4​π​Zi2​e2​ni/mi\omega_{pi}=\sqrt{4\pi Z_{i}^{2}e^{2}n_{i}/m_{i}} is the ion plasma frequency, Zi​eZ_{i}e is the ion charge, mim_{i} is its mass, nin_{i} is the ion number density, and a=(4πni/3)−1/3a=(4\pi n_{i}/3)^{-1/3} is the ion-sphere radius). The left vertical dotted line separates the regions of non-relativistic degenerate electrons (ve≪cv_{e}\ll c, ρ≪106\rho\ll 10^{6} g cm-3) and ultrarelativistic electrons (ve→cv_{e}\to c, ρ≫106\rho\gg 10^{6} g cm-3). The shaded regions I–IV show the temperature-density domains with the different regimes of e​eee collisions in a degenerate electron gas (see Section III, Table 1).

In order to explore the importance of the e​eee collisions for thermal conduction let us compare κe​e\kappa_{ee} with the thermal conductivity κe​i\kappa_{ei} owing to e​iei collisions (Section I). The conductivity κe​i\kappa_{ei} is calculated using the formalism of Potekhin et al. [12] and Gnedin et al. [6].

In Figure 2 we plot the temperature dependence of the electron thermal conductivity of helium (4He) or carbon (12C) plasmas at ρ=105\rho=10^{5} g cm-3 (left) or 10610^{6} g cm-3 (right). At ρ=105\rho=10^{5} g cm-3 the electrons are nonrelativistic while at ρ=106\rho=10^{6} g cm-3 they are mildly relativistic. According to Eq. (2), the total electron thermal conductivity κe\kappa_{e} is determined by the partial contributions κe​e\kappa_{ee} and κe​i\kappa_{ei}, a minimum partial contribution being most important. The total conductivities are shown by the solid lines; κe​i\kappa_{ei} by the dot-and-dashed lines; κe​e\kappa_{ee} is plotted by the dashed lines (the same for the helium and carbon plasmas); the dotted lines give κe​e\kappa_{ee} neglecting the contribution of transverse plasmons (i.e., by setting I=IlI=I_{l}).

For the densities and temperatures displayed in Figure 2, the e​iei collisions are mainly more efficient than the e​eee ones, although the contribution of the e​eee collisions into the total thermal conductivity is noticeable. One can see that the e​iei collisions are more important for heavier elements (because the Coulomb e​iei scattering cross section is much higher than the e​eee scattering cross section for high-ZZ elements; see Lampe [13]). The e​eee collisions would be negligible for the iron plasma if the data for this plasma were displayed in Figure 2. The e​eee collisions are more efficient in the helium plasma than in the carbon plasma because the helium ions have lower charges. For a given chemical composition, κe​e\kappa_{ee} gives highest contribution into κe\kappa_{e} at temperatures TT a few times lower than Tp​eT_{pe} (we have log10⁡Tp​e​[K]≈7.86\log_{10}T_{pe}{\rm[K]}\approx 7.86 and 8.32 at ρ=105\rho=10^{5} and 10610^{6} g cm-3, respectively). These temperatures separate the high-temperature and low-temperature e​eee collision regimes (e.g., the regimes I and II in the non-relativistic electron gas, see Table 1). For ρ=105\rho=10^{5} g cm-3, the electron gas is only slightly relativistic. Accordingly, the contribution of the Landau damping (transverse plasmons) into κe​e\kappa_{ee} is relatively small, and the results of Lampe [13] are sufficiently accurate. For higher ρ=106\rho=10^{6} g cm-3, the contribution of the Landau damping becomes more important which invalidates the previous results of Refs. [14, 15]. In this case the Landau damping strongly reduces κe​e\kappa_{ee} which makes the e​eee collisions much more important for thermal conduction than it was thought before. For still higher ρ\rho the contribution of κe​e\kappa_{ee} into κe\kappa_{e} in a plasma of light elements at T∼Tp​eT\sim T_{pe} would be even more significant. However, the temperature Tp​eT_{pe} would become so high that light elements would start burning in thermonuclear reactions. Therefore, e​eee collisions can noticeably decrease the electron thermal conductivity at densities and temperatures important for nuclear burning of light elements (for instance, in the vicinity of the carbon ignition curve). This should be taken into account in simulations of nuclear evolution of stars (e.g., carbon ignition in white dwarfs [4]).

Figure 3 shows the density dependence of the electron thermal conductivity in the density range from ∼2.5×109\sim 2.5\times 10^{9} g cm-3 to 101410^{14} g cm-3 for the three values of the temperature T=107T=10^{7}, 10810^{8}, and 10910^{9} K. We employ the same model of ground-state matter as in Figure 1. The displayed density range is appropriate to a crust of a neutron star. The vertical dotted line is the neutron drip point which separates the crust into the outer and inner parts. The adopted values of TT and ρ\rho refer to the regime IV of the e​eee collisions, where the electron gas is ultrarelativistic, T≪Tp​eT\ll T_{pe}, and the Landau damping dominates. The conductivity κe​e\kappa_{ee} (the dashed line) is well approximated by the temperature independent conductivity (20) governed by the Landau damping; κe​e\kappa_{ee} slightly deviates from Eq. (20) only at lowest ρ\rho for T=109T=10^{9} in Figure 3, where TT is still insufficiently lower than Tp​eT_{pe} (see Figure 1). Retaining the longitudinal contribution into κe​e\kappa_{ee} (I=IlI=I_{l}) and setting T=108T=10^{8} K, we would get the dotted curve in Fig. 3. It goes much higher than the dashed curve indicating that this longitudinal contribution is really insignificant.

For comparison, the dot-and-dashed lines in Figure 3 give the thermal conductivity κe​i\kappa_{ei} (mostly from Figure 4 of Ref. [6]) for the same values of TT, and the solid lines give the total conductivity κe\kappa_{e}. For T=108T=10^{8} and 10910^{9}, the effects of possible impurities in dense matter (atomic nuclei with charge numbers ZimpZ_{\rm imp} different from charge numbers ZiZ_{i} of ground-state nuclei) are expected to be small (e.g., Gnedin et al. [6]). At T=107T=10^{7} K, the effects of impurities can be substantial. For this TT in Figure 3 we present κe​i\kappa_{ei} and κe\kappa_{e} for pure ground-state matter and also for the matter which contains impurities with |Zimp−Zi|=2|Z_{\rm imp}-Z_{i}|=2 and with the fractional number of impurity nuclei of nimp/ni=0.05n_{\rm imp}/n_{i}=0.05. The impurities increase the e​iei collision rate and decrease the conductivities κe​i\kappa_{ei} and κe\kappa_{e}.

As seen from Figure 3, κe​i\kappa_{ei} is more important than κe​e\kappa_{ee} at all displayed densities for T=108T=10^{8} and 10910^{9} K. In these cases κe≈κe​i\kappa_{e}\approx\kappa_{ei} and we do not show κe\kappa_{e} to simplify the figure. However, κe​e\kappa_{ee} dominates in the pure ground-state matter for T=107T=10^{7} K at ρ≳1012\rho\gtrsim 10^{12} g cm-3 (in the inner crust of a neutron star). This dominance is fully produced by the Landau damping of transverse plasmons in the e​eee-collisions. For ρ≳1013\rho\gtrsim 10^{13} g cm-3 in this case we have κe≈κe​e\kappa_{e}\approx\kappa_{ee}. For an impure cold-catalyzed matter κe​i\kappa_{ei} remains important for all densities at T=107T=10^{7} K, but κe​e\kappa_{ee} is comparable to κe​i\kappa_{ei} in the inner neutron star crust. Note that the values of κe​i\kappa_{ei} in Figure 3 take into account, in an approximate manner, the freezing of Umklapp processes in electron-phonon scattering at low temperatures (see, e.g., Ref. [6]). For T≳108T\gtrsim 10^{8} K the freezing is unimportant, but at T∼107T\sim 10^{7} K it enhances κe​i\kappa_{ei}. A more rigorous treatment of this freezing can partly remove this enhancement (A. I. Chugunov, private communication), which can somewhat decrease κe​i\kappa_{ei} and reduce the importance of κe​e\kappa_{ee}.

Therefore, a correct treatment of e​eee collisions can considerably reduce the electron thermal conductivity in a cold neutron star crust, with T∼107T\sim 10^{7} K. This can increase the time of heat diffusion from the inner crust to the surface [9]. In particular, the effect can be important for the propagation of thermal waves produced by pulsar glitches and for the emergence of these waves on the pulsar surface. The emergence can be, in principle, observed and give valuable information on the nature of pulsar glitches [8].

While calculating κe​e\kappa_{ee} we have taken into account only the electron contribution into the polarization functions Πl\Pi_{l} and Πt\Pi_{t} in Eq. (6) and neglected the ion contribution. As shown by Lampe [13] this is a good approximation at high temperatures T≳Z2​e2/(a​kB)T\gtrsim Z^{2}e^{2}/(ak_{\rm B}) at which the ions are weakly coupled and constitute a Boltzmann gas. The calculation of the ion polarization functions at lower TT (in the regime of strong ion coupling, in an ion liquid or solid) is a complicated problem whose detailed solution is still absent. We have also neglected the effects of strong magnetic fields which can greatly modify electron heat transport in strongly magnetized neutron star envelopes. These effects are numerous (e.g., Yakovlev and Kaminker [26]) and are subdivided into classical (owing to rapid electron Larmor rotation) and quantum ones (owing to the Landau quantization of electron motion in a magnetic field). In principle, a proper treatment of e​eee collisions in a strong magnetic field can be performed in the same framework of the dynamical plasma screening as used above. However, the problem becomes much more complicated because the electron polarization tensor in a magnetic field is anisotropic (depends on the relative orientations of the wavevector 𝒒\bm{q} and the magnetic field) and cannot be generally decomposed into purely longitudinal and transverse parts [21]. The effects of ion polarization and strong magnetic fields are outside the scope of the present paper.

V Conclusions

We have reconsidered the electron thermal conductivity κe​e\kappa_{ee} of degenerate electrons produced owing to the e​eee collisions taking into account the Landau damping due to the exchange of transverse plasmons (following the calculations of kinetic properties of quark plasma by Heiselberg and Pethick [17]). The Landau damping has been neglected in all previous calculations of κe​e\kappa_{ee}. We have analyzed the four regimes of the e​eee collisions in the degenerate electron gas (Section III, Table 1) and obtained analytic expressions for κe​e\kappa_{ee} which accurately approximate the results of numerical calculations of κe​e\kappa_{ee} in wide ranges of the temperature and density of the matter. These results can be applied to study thermal conduction of degenerate electrons in metals, semiconductors, in degenerate cores of evolved stars and white dwarfs, and in envelopes of neutron stars.

Our main conclusions are the following.

(1) The Landau damping strongly modifies κe​e\kappa_{ee} in a relativistic degenerate electron gas, at densities ρ≳106\rho\gtrsim 10^{6} g cm-3, but it is also quite noticeable at lower ρ\rho (for instance, at ρ=105\rho=10^{5} g cm-3, see Figure 2). The Landau damping increases the e​eee collision rate and decreases κe​e\kappa_{ee}, increasing the contribution of the e​eee collisions into the total electron thermal conductivity κe\kappa_{e}.

(2) The most dramatic effect of the Landau damping on κe​e\kappa_{ee} takes place at ρ≫106\rho\gg 10^{6} g cm-3 for temperatures TT much below the electron plasma temperature Tp​eT_{pe} (the regime IV, Table 1). In this case κe​e\kappa_{ee} shows a non-Fermi-liquid behavior; it becomes temperature independent and is described by the asymptotic expression (20).

(3) The conductivity κe​e\kappa_{ee} becomes comparable to the electron thermal conductivity κe​i\kappa_{ei} provided by the electron-ion collisions (and gives thus a noticeable contribution into the total conductivity κe\kappa_{e}) in a warm plasma of light (low-ZZ) ions at temperatures TT a few times lower than Tp​eT_{pe} (Figure 2). These conditions are typical for degenerate cores of white dwarfs and giant stars where thermonuclear burning of light elements can occur (particularly, in the vicinity of the carbon ignition curve).

(4) The conductivity κe​e\kappa_{ee} dominates over κe​i\kappa_{ei} and determines the total electron thermal conductivity κe\kappa_{e} of the dense pure cold-catalyzed matter at T∼107T\sim 10^{7} K and ρ≳1012\rho\gtrsim 10^{12} g cm-3 (in the inner crust of a cold neutron star, Figure 3). At these TT and ρ\rho the conductivity κe​e\kappa_{ee} is important even for impure cold-catalyzed matter. It can affect the propagation of thermal waves, excited in the inner neutron star crust during pulsar glitches, to the pulsar surface.

The electron conductivity κe\kappa_{e} operates also in neutron star cores, at ρ≳1.5×1014\rho\gtrsim 1.5\times 10^{14} g cm-3. This conductivity should also be reconsidered taking into account the Landau damping. Our present results cannot be directly applied to this case because in the cores the electrons collide efficiently at least with degenerate electrons, muons, and protons, and these collisions deserve a special study. We intend to analyze them in a subsequent publication.
